title: Understand a login flow — example plan
brief: An illustrative explanation of signing in to a private web app. This is a map to discuss, not an implemented or security-reviewed authentication design.
objective: Understand where sign-in happens, which parts keep track of the session, and how failure is explained.
success: You can trace a sign-in from the form to a private page.
You can explain what each part does without having to know the chosen framework.

now: Map the main sign-in path and session check
Explain the proposed technology roles and recovery behavior
later: Choose an established authentication integration after inspecting the project
Plan account creation, account recovery and any additional sign-in factors
out: Implementing a new password or token system from scratch

context.detail: This example assumes an app with an established sign-in service and a server-managed browser session.
context.source: Illustrative scenario; replace with the actual project architecture.

steps.title: Understand the existing sign-in setup
steps.summary: Read the app’s current authentication integration and constraints.
steps.why: An existing integration should guide the plan before adding another system.
steps.deliverable: A short map of the current components, ownership and unresolved choices.
acceptance: The map distinguishes observed behavior from assumptions.

steps.title: Trace the normal and failed journeys
steps.summary: Explain how the visitor moves from the form to a private page.
steps.why: The diagram makes hidden handoffs and recovery choices visible.
steps.deliverable: A layered sign-in diagram with readable explanations.
acceptance: Every connection has a plain-language explanation.
Failure and session-expiry behavior are shown.

steps.title: Review choices before implementation
steps.summary: Resolve the important assumptions with the project owner.
steps.why: A useful explanation is not proof that a design is ready for production.
steps.deliverable: A revised plan with project-specific verification requirements.
acceptance: The owner understands the chosen integration and its limitations.

diagrams.title: What happens when you sign in?
diagrams.description: One system, several connected groups. Visitor-facing screens, authentication services and recovery steps have their own nodes. Focus a layer to light up the relevant parts; the surrounding system stays visible in grey.

layers.title: Visitor journey
layers.description: Start with the visible action, then follow the handoffs until the app can show a private page.

nodes.detail: The form collects the required sign-in information and shows progress while the request is processed.
The server coordinates the sign-in flow using the established authentication integration.
After a successful sign-in, the app establishes a session so the visitor does not have to sign in on every page.

nodes.summary: The app checks access before showing data.
nodes.detail: Opening a private page still requires a server-side session and permission check. A hidden link alone does not protect the underlying data.

edges.label: Submit sign-in
edges.detail: The browser sends the sign-in request using the established integration.

edges.label: Establish a session
edges.detail: After successful identity verification, the app establishes the session.

edges.label: Open the private page
edges.detail: The app validates the session and access permissions before showing private information.

layers.title: Auth & data
layers.description: Names such as server, identity provider and session describe responsibilities. The actual products should come from the project, not from a default stack.

nodes.detail: Server-side code checks requests and permissions. Sensitive configuration belongs here rather than in code downloaded by every visitor.

nodes.summary: An established auth library or service.
nodes.detail: Prefer the app’s existing supported integration. Introducing a new provider affects migration, account ownership, cost and maintenance.

nodes.summary: Session mechanism: remember a signed-in visitor.
nodes.detail: In this illustrative server-session design, a browser cookie carries the session identifier. Cookie settings, expiry and request protection must follow the selected integration’s guidance.

nodes.summary: The identity system owns the account records.
nodes.detail: The selected authentication integration decides how account records are stored and looked up. The browser must not directly query credential storage. This node describes a responsibility, not a chosen database product.

edges.label: Use the auth integration
edges.detail: The app delegates identity verification to the supported integration.

edges.label: Look up the account
edges.detail: The identity system accesses its account records through its supported storage mechanism.

edges.label: Create and validate the session
edges.detail: The server uses the existing session mechanism to recognize the signed-in visitor.

layers.title: Failure & recovery
layers.description: Inspect the parts involved when sign-in fails or a session ends, while keeping the same map.

nodes.summary: Explain the failure and allow retry.
nodes.detail: Show a useful sign-in error without claiming success. Preserve appropriate non-sensitive input, and do not copy passwords into notes, logs or persistent drafts.
The server needs clear failure results, abuse controls and logging that avoids credentials. Details must be verified against the chosen integration.
When appropriate, guide the visitor back to sign-in and restore the intended destination afterward. Returning to a private URL must still enforce permissions.
Show a clear failure and a way to retry. Preserve appropriate non-sensitive inputs; do not copy passwords into persistent drafts or logs.

nodes.summary: Explain that sign-in is needed again.
nodes.detail: When the server rejects an expired session, protect the private content and guide the visitor back to sign-in. Re-check permissions when returning.

edges.label: Sign-in rejected or interrupted
edges.detail: Return a clear result without exposing credentials or claiming success.

edges.label: Try again
edges.detail: Return to the recoverable form with an explanation.

edges.label: Session is no longer valid
edges.detail: The server prevents access when the session has expired.

edges.label: Sign in again
edges.detail: Return to sign-in and preserve a safe intended destination when supported.
